title: What comes next?
objectives: Build a next-word table by counting the pairs of words in a text.

screens.title: What comes next?
screens.prose: Real chatbots run on huge networks, far bigger than the two layers you built. The idea underneath starts with counting. Here is a text of 20 words, counting each full stop as a word.
screens.question: Tap every word that comes straight after “the”.

hints.text: Find each “the”, then look one word to its right.
The first “the” is followed by “cat”.
“the” appears six times, so tap six words: cat, mat, cat, jam, dog and cat.

feedback.correct: Six words follow “the”: cat three times, and mat, jam and dog once each.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Tap only the word just to the right of each “the”.

byKey.the-itself: You tapped each “the”. Tap the word that comes straight after it instead.

explain.text: Each “the” is followed by one word: cat, mat, cat, jam, dog and cat. So in this text cat came after “the” 3 times in 6. For “the cat sat on the ...”, the text votes for cat.

screens.title: Walk the pairs
screens.prose: Slide through the text one **pair** at a time: a word and the word straight after it. The caption keeps a tally for the pairs that start with “the”.

screens.question: Fill in the row for “the”: how often each word follows it.

hints.text: Stop at each pair whose first word is “the”.
Pairs 1, 8 and 18 are “the cat”; pairs 5, 11 and 14 give mat, jam and dog.

feedback.correct: cat 3, mat 1, jam 1 and dog 1: six pairs start with “the”.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Step to each pair that starts with “the” and tally its second word.

byKey.cat-once: “the cat” comes three times: pairs 1, 8 and 18. Count every pair, not each different word.

explain.text: Six pairs start with “the”. Cat is the second word in three of them, and mat, jam and dog in one each.

screens.title: A next-word table
screens.prose: You just built one row of a **next-word table**. Each row is a word, and it counts the words that come straight after it. It is also called a **bigram table**: “bi” means two, and a bigram is a pair of words.
screens.question: How many times does “on” come straight after “sat”?

hints.text: Find each “sat” in the text.
Here are the two places “sat” appears.
Both are followed by “on”: 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find every “sat” and look at the word after it.

byKey.once: “sat” appears twice, and “on” follows both times. Count each pair.

explain.text: “sat” appears twice and “on” follows both times. So the row for “sat” is on 2 and nothing else.

screens.title: The row for cat
screens.prose: Now the row for “cat”. A word that never comes straight after “cat” gets a count of 0.
screens.question: Fill in the row for “cat”.

hints.text: “cat” appears three times. What comes straight after each?
The three places “cat” appears.
sat, ate and “.”, once each; “on” never follows “cat”.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Look only one word to the right of each “cat”.

byKey.two-on: “on” comes two words after “cat”, in “cat sat on”. The table counts only the word straight after.

explain.text: “cat” appears three times, followed by sat, ate and “.”. So its row has three words with count 1 each, and “on” gets 0.

screens.title: How many pairs?
screens.prose: Each pair starts at one word and ends at the next. The pairs overlap: “cat” ends the pair “the cat” and starts the pair “cat sat”.
screens.question: How many pairs does the 20-word text have?

hints.text: Does the last word start a pair?
The last word, “.”, has nothing after it.
Every word but the last starts one pair: 19.

feedback.correct: 19 pairs: every word except the last starts one.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the words that have a word after them.

byKey.per-word: The last word starts no pair, so it is one fewer than 20.
byKey.no-overlap: You cut the text into separate pairs. The pairs overlap, so each word but the last starts one.

explain.text: Every word except the last starts exactly one pair, so 20 words give 19 pairs. The pair counts in the whole table add up to 19 too.

screens.title: Which way round?
screens.prose: Here is the whole next-word table. A row is the word now and a column is the word straight after it.

state.caption: Row: the word now. Column: the word straight after it. A blank is 0.

screens.question: In the row for “cat”, what is the count in the column for “the”?

hints.text: In the pair “the cat”, which word comes first?
This is the row for “cat”.
After “cat” come sat, ate and “.”, never “the”: 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read along the row for “cat” to the column for “the”.

byKey.backwards: You read the pair “the cat” the wrong way round. That pair sits in the row for “the”, in the column for “cat”.

explain.text: The row for “cat” lists what comes after “cat”: sat, ate and “.”, once each. The word before “cat” is always “the”, and that is counted in the row for “the”.

screens.title: An empty row
screens.prose: The last word of a text has no word after it. Our last “.” starts no pair, but “.” still has a row from the earlier full stops. Now take a shorter text.
screens.question: Which word has an empty row in the next-word table of this text?

options.why: “the” is followed by dog and by mat, so its row has two words.

hints.text: Which word never has a word after it?
Look at the end of the text.
“mat” comes only at the end, so no pair starts with it.

feedback.correct: mat: it appears only as the last word.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find a word that never starts a pair.

byKey.the: “the” starts two pairs, “the dog” and “the mat”.

explain.text: “mat” is the last word and appears nowhere else, so no pair starts with it. Its row is empty, and a writer that reaches “mat” has no next word to choose.

screens.title: Counting pairs in code
screens.prose: `sorted(pairs)` returns the list in order: pairs sort by their first word, then their second. The starter makes the sorted pairs. Equal pairs then sit side by side, so one pass can count them.
screens.question: Finish `count_pairs(words)`: return a list of `(first, second, count)`, sorted by first word, then second.

widget.starter:
def count_pairs(words):
    pairs = []
    for i in range(len(words) - 1):
        pairs.append((words[i], words[i + 1]))
    pairs = sorted(pairs)
    result = []
    # walk the sorted pairs and count each run of equal pairs
    return result

Cuts the text into separate pairs instead of overlapping ones, so half the pairs are missed.
Lists every pair with count 1 instead of counting each run of equal pairs.

hints.text: Walk `pairs` with `for p in pairs:` and compare `p` with the last triple in `result`.
If `p` has the same two words as `result[-1]`, add 1 to its count; else append `(p[0], p[1], 1)`.

feedback.correct: Your function counts each run of equal pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: `['a', 'a', 'a']` has two overlapping pairs, both `('a', 'a')`: one triple with count 2.

screens.title: The whole table
screens.prose: A next-word table counts every pair: $$\text{count}(a \to b) = \text{places where } b \text{ comes straight after } a$$ A text of $n$ words has $n - 1$ pairs, and each pair adds 1 to one cell.
screens.question: A text has 101 words. What do all the counts in its next-word table add up to?

hints.text: How many pairs does a text of 101 words have?
101 − 1 = 100 pairs, one count each.

feedback.correct: 100: one count for each of the 100 pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each pair adds 1 to exactly one cell.

byKey.per-word: The last word starts no pair, so there are 100 pairs, not 101.

explain.text: A text of 101 words has 100 pairs, and each adds 1 to exactly one cell. So the counts add to 100, one fewer than the words.

screens.title: A trader's keyboard
screens.prose: Early phone keyboards suggested your next word from a giant table of this kind. A trader's phone has counted the words after “sell” in her messages: shares 14, the 9, now 5, short 2.
screens.question: How many pairs in her messages start with “sell”?

hints.text: Each count is a number of pairs that start with “sell”.
Add every bar.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the four counts.

byKey.different: 4 is the number of different words. Add their counts.
byKey.top: 14 is only the pairs “sell shares”. Add the other words too.

explain.text: The row for “sell” holds $14 + 9 + 5 + 2 = 30$ pairs, so the keyboard offers shares first, then the. Modern keyboards use small networks instead, trained on the same kind of examples.

ideas: A next-word table counts, for each word, how often each word comes straight after it.
A text of $n$ words has $n - 1$ pairs, because the last word starts none.
A row is the word now: the row for “cat” counts what follows “cat”, not what comes before it.

formula.name: Pairs in a text
formula.note: For a text of $n$ words. The counts in the whole table add to the same number.

summary.trap: Reading the table the wrong way round: the pair “the cat” is counted in the row for “the”, not the row for “cat”.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Every word but the last starts a pair.

explain.text: Each of the first six words starts one pair, so the text has 6 pairs.

quiz.prose: Take the same text, `up up down up down down up`.
quiz.question: How many times does “down” come straight after “up”?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Look one word to the right of each “up”.

byKey.downs: 3 counts every “down”, but one of them follows another “down”.

explain.text: The pairs are `up up`, `up down`, `down up`, `up down`, `down down` and `down up`. So `up down` appears 2 times.

quiz.prose: A next-word table is built from a long text.
quiz.question: What does the row for “on” hold?

options.text: Counts of the words straight after “on”
Counts of the words straight before “on”
options.why: That reads pairs the wrong way round. A word before “on” is counted in that word's own row.

options.text: Counts of every word in a sentence with “on”
options.why: The table counts neighbouring pairs only, not whole sentences.

feedback.correct: The row for “on” counts what comes straight after it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A row is the word now.

explain.text: A row is the word now and its columns are the words that come straight after it. So the row for “on” counts the words that follow “on”.
